992: 6. Obtaining solubility ranges and the phase diagram from the competition of all phases
993: Stage 06 in Fig. 1 is the stage that determines phase equilibria from the free energies of all phases. It is not restricted to calphy. For composition-resolved free energies of a binary system there is a route that uses calphy's phase-diagram functions, explained in the worked example below. When a CALPHAD model is used, an equilibrium code such as pycalphad is used. The convex hull and common tangents can also be computed in-house. MD and thermodynamic integration with calphy belong to the stage that produces each phase's free energy; their role differs from the all-phase equilibrium calculation of 06. Check whether the chosen equilibrium method covers internal site fractions of ordered phases, candidate phases and multicomponent systems.
995: At fixed temperature, pressure and overall composition it finds the combination of phases that minimises the total Gibbs free energy of the system. It does not merely pick the lowest phase at the same composition; it also compares states split into several phases of different compositions. Ordinary bulk phase equilibria neglect interfacial energy.
996: For a binary system with overall B atom fraction x₀, the minimisation can be written as follows.
997: g is the Gibbs free energy per atom of each phase, f is the phase fraction on an atom basis, and x is the B atom fraction of that phase. Eq. (H7) states the conditions that the phase fractions sum to one and that composition is conserved. The composition of a line phase is fixed; for phases with a composition range the composition is also a variable. In a sublattice model the internal site fractions of each phase are either included in the minimisation or a phase free energy minimised beforehand is used.
998: Illustrative example: even at an overall composition of 0.5, composition is conserved if an α phase with B atom fraction 0.2 and a β phase with 0.8 are present in equal halves on an atom basis. If the following holds at the same temperature and pressure, the two-phase state α + β is favoured over the single phase γ.
999: In Eq. (H8) the temperature and pressure arguments are omitted. These compositions are for illustration only and are not coexistence compositions obtained from an actual calculation. Moreover, this inequality is only a comparison with γ; to establish the true equilibrium, all combinations of candidate phases and compositions must be examined. The lower convex hull and common tangents of a binary system are the graphical form of this free-energy minimisation.
1000: At each temperature and pressure, the lower convex hull of g(T,P,x) over all phases is computed. The equilibrium at overall composition x̄ is the following constrained minimisation. f<sub>φ</sub> is the phase fraction on an atom basis.
1001: The coexistence compositions of two smooth phases α and β satisfy the common-tangent condition. The derivatives are taken at fixed T and P.
1002: The common tangent must support the whole free-energy set from below, including the other phases. A line phase is treated as a point of fixed composition, and no g′ is required at that point.
1003: The solubility range is the composition range in which that phase is stable as a single phase. It differs from the width of the two-phase region, from the input composition range, and from the range over which the structure survives relaxation. The solubility limit is not fixed by the configurational entropy alone; the free energies of the competing phases are also needed.
1004: The coexistence compositions are tracked temperature by temperature to draw the T–x phase diagram. One can choose either the route that computes the convex hull directly, or the route that fits a CALPHAD form, writes a TDB and solves the equilibrium with pycalphad or similar. For models that generate the ideal-mixing term automatically, fit only the reference and excess terms to avoid double counting.
1005: A concrete example of computing a two-phase region
1006: At fixed temperature and pressure, the two ends of the common tangent are the compositions of the coexisting phases. For overall compositions in between, the phase fractions change according to the lever rule. Determining and connecting the coexistence compositions at each temperature draws the boundaries of the two-phase region. Distinguish the solubility range of a single phase from the composition width of the two-phase region.

1027: Algorithms when no interpolation function (CALPHAD type) is used
1028: The only CALPHAD-type element of this workflow is the choice of function that interpolates between sample points (ideal mixing + Redlich–Kister, CEF-type sublattice). The phase equilibrium itself is the lower convex hull of stage 06 (common tangents, Eqs. (H1)–(H5)), a procedure that needs no analytic function. Without the interpolation function, the algorithms fall into the following two families.
1029: A. Use no function and take the equilibrium directly from the sample points (within 05 → 06). (1) At each temperature, connect each phase's sample points (x_i, G_i ± σ_i) as they are, or with a σ-weighted smoothing spline. Terms known analytically (ideal mixing (E1), sublattice s_conf (E10)–(E12)) are exact counting expressions, not CALPHAD, and are kept separate (otherwise the interpolation cannot reproduce the x ln x end-point shape and sample noise turns into spurious miscibility gaps; section 9, 04A/06). (2) Take the lower convex hull of the point set of all phases. The tangent end points are sample points themselves, so the boundary resolution is set by the sample spacing, and the error is propagated from σ_i by Monte Carlo. (3) Add sample points near the boundaries and recompute (adaptive sampling). In ftphase this is builder_from_table(fit="spline" | "smooth"); the price is that sample noise becomes curvature directly, so spurious same-phase intervals appear easily (in practice, intervals that do not move under Monte Carlo are classed as noise).
1030: B. Build no free-energy curves and find the equilibrium directly by simulation (replacing 06).

1059: The strength of family B is that it needs neither an interpolation function nor an assumption about short-range order, and short-range order and defect interactions enter automatically. Its weaknesses are that each boundary point needs MC/MD (a Δμ × T sweep), that solid–liquid transitions rarely occur during a simulation so TI or the interface method is needed separately, and that the width of ordered phases requires a sublattice analysis in post-processing. This workflow is family A (table of 05 + analytic entropy terms → convex hull of 06), and rk is merely the choice for connecting the 11 liquid compositions smoothly. If it is replaced, a σ-weighted smoothing spline is the smallest change. Family B is tried as route B (direct SGC MC, Ag–Cu) and its boundaries are compared with family A (fcc gap from ideal mixing + RK). The difference between the two is an estimate of the error from short-range order and the interpolation function.
1060: 7. Convergence, errors and artefacts to keep
1061: Solid phases: check displacement amplitude, supercell, q-points, volume points, force-constant fit, imaginary modes and configuration samples.
1062: Liquid phase: check number of atoms, MD time step, equilibration time, switching time, repetitions, forward–backward difference, diffusion and stationarity.
1063: Phase equilibria: add composition points near the phase boundaries and vary the free-energy uncertainty to probe the sensitivity of the boundaries.
1064: Common reference: check normalisation per atom, pressure, elemental references, and duplication or omission of configurational, vibrational and quantum contributions.
1065: At minimum, save phase, x, T, P, g, uncertainty, volume, method, reference_state, model/version. Link the structures, SQS conditions, MCP inputs, AiiDA pks, MD and phonon settings, fit expressions and rerun commands. If converted to a TDB, compare whether the original g and phase boundaries are reproduced.
